current_example.title: Example: Evaluating a Triple Integral by Converting to Cylindrical Coordinates

q-161613.name: Question 1
q-161613.problem:
The region $R$ is enclosed inside the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ for $x\le 0$ and $y\ge 0,$ between the surfaces $z=0$ and $z=\sqrt{4-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}.$ Express the following triple integral in cylindrical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}\text{d}V
$$
q-161613.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,z)\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14131107/assets/8dc4ea0ad2bb776fb31132e1ff8d97efdd2c166dc23ffbc8641f8d7034b8d487.png)

The region $R$ is one-quarter of a right vertical cylinder of radius $1$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=0,$ and

- bounded above by $z=\sqrt{4-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}=\sqrt{4-{r}^{2}}.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta ,z)\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi ,\,0\le z\le \sqrt{4-{r}^{2}}\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\text{d}V & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-{r}^{2}}}r\,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

The region R is enclosed inside the cylinder x2+y2=1 for x≤0 and y≥0, between the surfaces z=0 and z=4−(x2+y2). Express the following triple integral in cylindrical polar coordinates. ∭RdV

a
∫π/2π∫01∫04−rrdzdrdθ
b
∫0π∫01∫04−rr2dzdrdθ
c
∫π/2π∫01∫04−r2rdzdrdθ
d
∫0π∫01∫04−r2rdzdrdθ
e
∫π/2π∫01∫04−r2r2dzdrdθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the change of variables formula in the form ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∭Δf(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ,z)rdzdrdθ.

If (r,θ,z) are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates (x,y,z) can be found by using the formulas

x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ,z=z.

First, let's sketch the projection of R onto the xy-plane:

The region R is one-quarter of a right vertical cylinder of radius 1 whose axis passes through the point (0,0) in the xy-plane, and is

  • bounded below by z=0, and

  • bounded above by z=4−(x2+y2)=4−r2.

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as Δ={(r,θ,z):0≤r≤1,π2≤θ≤π,0≤z≤4−r2}.

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

∭RdV=∫π/2π∫01∫04−r2rdzdrdθ.

q-161604.name: Question 2
q-161604.problem:
The region $R$ is enclosed inside the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ between the surfaces $z=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ and $z=3.$ Express the following triple integral in cylindrical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V
$$
q-161604.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,z)\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14131107/assets/9c4ea0ba92e19a201e3944defa6deb0bc1ee76971adaa809521722b6ac31241f.png)

The region $R$ is a right vertical cylinder of radius $3$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}=r,$ and

- bounded above by $z=3.$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta ,z)\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,0\le \theta <2\pi ,\,r\le z\le 3\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\cdot r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={∭}_{Δ}r\sqrt{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{r}^{3}{r}^{2}\,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

b

c

We will use the change of variables formula in the form ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∭Δf(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ,z)rdzdrdθ.

If (r,θ,z) are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates (x,y,z) can be found by using the formulas

x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ,z=z.

First, let's sketch the projection of R onto the xy-plane:

The region R is a right vertical cylinder of radius 3 whose axis passes through the point (0,0) in the xy-plane, and is

  • bounded below by z=x2+y2=r, and

  • bounded above by z=3.

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as Δ={(r,θ,z):0≤r≤3,0≤θ<2π,r≤z≤3}.

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

∭Rx2+y2dV=∭Δ(rcos⁡θ)2+(rsin⁡θ)2⋅rdzdrdθ=∭Δrr2(cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ)dzdrdθ=∫02π∫03∫r3r2dzdrdθ.

q-161637.problem:
If the solid region $R$ is given by 

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+(y-4)^{2}\le 16,\,x\ge 0,\,-5\le z\le x\},
$$

then ${∭}_{R}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}V=$
q-161637.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,z)\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14131107/assets/b66b8db18b2f5773addc2d00c02f2f15f4a7ead53323418e63bd50457f74466b.png)

The region $R$ is one-half of a right vertical cylinder of radius $4$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,4)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=-5,$ and

- bounded above by $z=x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+(y-4)^{2}=16$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+(y-4)^{2} & =16 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -4)^{2} & =16 \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -8r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +16 & =16 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-8r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-8r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-8\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=8\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta ,z)\,:\,0\le r\le 8\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},\,-5\le z\le r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+1}\cdot r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={∭}_{Δ}\sqrt{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+1}\cdot r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{8\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\int }_{-5}^{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }r\sqrt{{r}^{2}+1}\,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

q-161633.problem:
If the solid region $R$ is given by 

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+(y-2)^{2}\le 4,\,x\le 0,\,-2\le z\le \sqrt{16-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}\},
$$

then ${∭}_{R}2xy\,\text{d}V=$
q-161633.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,z)\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14131107/assets/831de8cf1d9833f8674a7e4cb69d01098970eefb9cf576c0537fa7be471c8c2c.png)

The region $R$ is one-half of a right vertical cylinder of radius $2$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,2)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=-2,$ and

- bounded above by $z=\sqrt{16-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}=\sqrt{16-{r}^{2}}.$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+(y-2)^{2}=4$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+(y-2)^{2} & =4 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -2)^{2} & =4 \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -4r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4 & =4 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-4r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-4r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta ,z)\,:\,0\le r\le 4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi ,\,-2\le z\le \sqrt{16-{r}^{2}}\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}2xy\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}2(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\cdot r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\int }_{-2}^{\sqrt{16-{r}^{2}}}{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

q-161608.name: Question 5
q-161608.problem:
Evaluate the triple integral 

$$
{∭}_{R}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}V
$$

over the region $R$ enclosed inside the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ and between the surfaces $z=0$ and $z=4-x.$
q-161608.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,z)\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

If $(r,\theta ,z)$ are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the formulas

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z=z.
$$

First, let's sketch the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14131107/assets/62abd56d2d374afb7c608aa64f701cfe94f096b823f964697a929c7c24f3a073.png)

The region $R$ is a right vertical cylinder of radius $1$ whose axis passes through the point $(0,0)$ in the $xy$-plane, and is

- bounded below by $z=0,$ and

- bounded above by $z=4-x=4-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta ,z)\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,0\le \theta <2\pi ,\,0\le z\le 4-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}({(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2})\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{4-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{r}^{3}\,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}[z]_{z=0}^{z=4-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}(4-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}4{r}^{3}-{r}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[{r}^{4}-\frac{1}{5}{r}^{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]}_{r=0}^{r=1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }1-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =[\theta -\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =2\pi } \\  & =(2\pi -0)-\frac{1}{5}(0-0) \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}(x-y)\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}{\int }_{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }^{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +9}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,dz\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )[z]_{z=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }^{z=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +9}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +9-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}9{r}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}[3{r}^{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )]_{r=0}^{r=\sqrt{3}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}3(\sqrt{3})^{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}9\sqrt{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =9\sqrt{3}[\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]_{\theta =-\pi /2}^{\theta =\pi /2} \\  & =9\sqrt{3}(1-(-1))+9\sqrt{3}(0-0) \\  & =18\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the triple integral ∭R(x−y)dV over the region R enclosed inside the cylinder x2+y2=3 for x≥0 and between the surfaces z=x and z=9+x.

EXPLANATION

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∭Δf(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ,z)rdzdrdθ.

If (r,θ,z) are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates (x,y,z) can be found by using the formulas

x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ,z=z.

First, let's sketch the projection of R onto the xy-plane:

The region R is a right vertical cylinder of radius 3 whose axis passes through the point (0,0) in the xy-plane, and is

  • bounded below by z=x=rcos⁡θ, and

  • bounded above by z=x+9=rcos⁡θ+9.

As a result, in cylindrical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as

Δ={(r,θ,z):0≤r≤3,−π2≤θ<π2,rcos⁡θ≤z≤rcos⁡θ+9}.

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain
